summary: For ages 5–7, build the understanding that teen numbers (11–19) are 'a ten and some ones' — the first appearance of place value. The central move is unitising: bundling ten single ones into one TEN unit the child can see and handle, then recognising the extras. Learners should compose teens (14 = 10 + 4) and decompose them (16 → 10 + 6), record equations both ways, and connect the written numeral to the grouped quantity so the '1' in 14 reads as one TEN. Confront the language trap directly: 'eleven'/'twelve' hide the ten, and 'thir-teen' says the ones first, while the numeral 1_ shows the ten first.
misconceptions: Seeing a teen number as a heap of individual ones, with no 'ten' unit (no place-value structure yet).
Reading the numeral literally as two ones ('one, four' for 14) rather than 'one ten and four'.
Teen word transposition (thirteen → 31) from the ones-first naming.
Thinking 'eleven' and 'twelve' are unrelated to ten because the words give no clue.
Miscounting the ten (treating the ten-rod as one object = 1, so 14 becomes 5) — unitising confusion.

activities.title: Make a ten and the leftovers
steps: Count out loose counters for a teen number such as 14.
Fill a ten-frame by placing counters one at a time until the frame holds ten.
Once ten are grouped, treat the full frame (or a ten-bead bar / Dienes ten-rod) as ONE 'ten' unit; put the remaining counters in a second frame.
Say the result aloud: 'one ten and four ones'.
Repeat with 13, 16, 17, 19, each time grouping exactly ten and naming the leftovers.
activities.insight: A teen number is not a heap of single ones — ten of them bundle into one 'ten' unit, and the rest are the extra ones. This bundling (unitising) is the seed of all place value.

activities.title: Compose and decompose, both ways
steps: Compose: 'Build 16 from a ten and some ones' — make one ten, add 6 extras, then write 16 = 10 + 6.
Decompose: start with 18 shown as a ten and extras; break the ten back into ten single ones and write 18 = 10 + 8.
Do several in each direction, recording the equation each time (13 = 10 + 3, 17 = 10 + 7).
Explain in words: 'Thirteen is one ten and three ones.'
activities.insight: Teen numbers can be put together from a ten and some ones and taken apart again; the equation 14 = 10 + 4 captures this part–whole structure flexibly in both directions.

activities.title: The numeral shows what the word hides
steps: Lay the grouped quantity (a ten unit + extras) beside the written numeral, e.g. 14.
Point to the '1' and say what it stands for: 'This is the one TEN I bundled, not one.'
Point to the '4' and tie it to the leftover ones.
Say the number word 'fourteen' and notice it says 'four' first even though the numeral writes the ten first; then say 'thir-teen' and notice the same ones-first naming.
Say 'eleven' and 'twelve' and note the words give no clue about the ten — only the model and numeral reveal it.
activities.insight: The written numeral 1_ shows the ten-first structure, while teen words either hide the ten (eleven, twelve) or say the ones first (thir-teen). Anchoring meaning to the ten-and-ones model guards against reading 14 as 'one and four' and against writing thirteen as 31.

activities.title: Explain and check with a diagnostic prompt
steps: Put out 14 counters (or another teen quantity) and answer: 'How is 14 made up out of tens and ones? Show me with the counters and tell me how you know.'
Make one group of ten, read the leftover four, and state '14 = 10 + 4'.
Answer probes: 'Make a group of ten — how many are left over?', 'How is 14 different from 41?', 'Show 17 as a ten and some ones and write it as 10 + 7.'
activities.insight: Independently describing a teen number as one ten and some ones, and linking it to the numeral, is the sign the ten is now seen as a unit within the number.

checkQuestion: Put out 14 counters. Ask: 'How is 14 made up out of tens and ones? Show me with the counters and tell me how you know.'
checkAnswer: 14 is one ten and four ones. Group ten counters into a ten; four are left over, so 14 = 10 + 4.
